strengths: The paper identifies a useful limitation of curricula that always increase team size: additional agents can make cooperative tasks easier. Jointly adapting agent count and environment variables through self-paced learning is a well-motivated application of existing methodology.

Figure 3 provides substantive evidence of improved target-task performance in Pursuit, with five runs and standard-deviation bands. Increasing and decreasing curricula, EPC/VACL comparisons, and separate agent-count and grid-size ablations strengthen this experiment.
Visualizing the learned curricula helps interpret the method. Reporting the limited benefits on Simple-Spread and Simple-Push is valuable and makes the task dependence of the results visible.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of task difficulty is insufficiently supported. Section 4.3 defines difficulty through improvement achievable in one policy update, whereas Equation (3) changes the context distribution to maximize estimated return for a fixed policy. High return does not establish rapid learning or useful transfer, particularly when reward magnitudes differ across contexts. Direct measurements of learning progress and transfer are needed to support the claimed interpretation of the curricula.

The Sum-versus-Average discussion overstates what the experiment establishes. For a fixed team size N, dividing a shared reward by N preserves the cooperative objective. Across team sizes, it changes the relative weighting of contexts in the curriculum objective. Figure 5 therefore demonstrates sensitivity to reward normalization; it does not establish that averaging introduces competition or discourages cooperation. Controls for reward scale and the performance threshold would help distinguish these explanations.

The methodological change largely applies the existing SPRL objective from [10] to agent count, so the contribution depends substantially on the empirical insights. Clear benefits are concentrated in one Pursuit configuration with a target of ten agents, using parameter-sharing IPPO. The explanations involving collisions and transfer in the MPE tasks are not tested through controlled interventions, and scaling to substantially larger target teams is not demonstrated. This limits support for the broader conclusions about when agent-count curricula help.

Training-budget fairness is unclear. The learning curves report 'steps' without specifying whether these count joint environment transitions or individual-agent transitions. Because IPPO pools experience from a changing number of agents, equal environment steps can imply different amounts of training data. Reporting both sample counts and computational cost would clarify the efficiency gains. A matched random-context curriculum would also help isolate adaptive selection from the benefits of training across easier contexts.

Important reproduction details are missing despite the appendix tables, including the task-specific performance threshold V_LB, network widths, and precise implementation of the curriculum value estimate using IPPO's local observations and rewards. The EPC/VACL adaptations and handling of bounded, discretized Gaussian contexts also need fuller specification. These choices directly affect the reported curriculum behavior.

The introduction's statement that SPMARL 'guarantees convergence to comparable performance' is unsupported by a convergence argument; the experiments establish only observed outcomes in the tested settings. More minor presentation issues include inconsistent old/new distribution notation around Equation (2) and incorrect figure references in the appendix.
